About the Catalogue

How We Curate Northern Dial

The artist library is a living editorial resource, not an automated scrape. Northern Dial reviews artist identities, removes clearly non-Canadian or non-artist credits, enriches profiles with reliable sources and keeps ambiguous cases unresolved until the evidence is strong enough.

ReviewArtist credits are checked rather than accepted blindly from source metadata.
VerifyProfiles use reliable sources, official links and location information where available.
RemoveClearly non-Canadian artists and non-artist credits are excluded from the public artist index.
Resolve CarefullyUncertain cases stay unresolved instead of being turned into confident guesses.

2 Versatile is a Canadian old-school hip-hop act whose self-titled album appeared in 1994. The group is part of the early Canadian rap catalogue and is associated with recordings including Cuddle with Me, which features Canadian R&B singer Glenn Lewis. Northern Dial carries 2 Versatile as part of that 1990s Canadian hip-hop lineage.

2Rude (3 tracks)

Toronto producer and Rudimental Records founder 2Rude helped build the connective tissue of Canadian hip-hop and R&B in the late 1990s and early 2000s. His Rudimental 2K project brought Canadian and U.S. artists together, while "Thinkin' About You" won the 2000 Juno for Best R&B/Soul Recording. His work with Maestro, Jully Black, Saukrates and others made him an important behind-the-scenes architect of Toronto's urban-music ecosystem.

Toronto, Ontario

4KORNERS (2 tracks)

Toronto DJ and producer 4KORNERS has spent years connecting Canadian music, nightlife and basketball culture as the Toronto Raptors' official DJ. His 2022 debut album 4KORNERS of the World translated that global club experience into a genre-spanning portrait of multicultural Toronto, with emerging Canadian artists placed at the centre. His significance lies as much in curation and platform-building as in production: he has used major stages to introduce audiences to new domestic music.

Toronto, Ontario

54•40 (3 tracks)

Vancouver-area rock band 54•40 grew from early-1980s post-punk and college rock into one of Canada's most durable alternative-radio institutions. Show Me opened the national breakthrough, while platinum albums Dear Dear, Smilin' Buddha Cabaret and Trusted by Millions produced staples such as "Nice to Luv You" and "Ocean Pearl." Their song "I Go Blind" later reached a much larger U.S. audience through Hootie & the Blowfish, but 54•40's real legacy is a four-decade Canadian catalogue connecting underground roots with mainstream rock.

Vancouver, British Columbia

Montréal-born artist and producer Charlie Kunce-Belhadj records as A Girl Named Sue, an independent project moving between electronic pop, drum and bass and intimate songwriting. Her self-produced approach makes A Girl Named Sue a notable emerging Montréal voice to follow as the catalogue develops.

Ottawa’s A Tribe Called Red, now The Halluci Nation, transformed Canadian electronic music by bringing powwow singing and drums into club, hip-hop and bass production. Nation II Nation and We Are the Halluci Nation made contemporary Indigenous identity central rather than decorative, while their national visibility helped widen space for Indigenous artists across modern Canadian genres.

A-Trak (4 tracks)

Montréal-born A-Trak went from teenage turntablism champion to one of the key connectors between hip-hop and electronic music. After winning the 1997 DMC World DJ Championship, he toured with Kanye West, co-founded Fool's Gold Records and later reached global pop audiences with Duck Sauce's “Barbra Streisand.” His career helped move DJ culture from battle craft into label-building, production and international festival music.

Adelaide (2 tracks)

Adelaide is an alternate Northern Dial library credit created when the name of Oshawa, Ontario band Mary & Adelaide is split at the ampersand. The exact Northern Dial tracks 'Hoodie zipper' and 'You pulled up' both come from the Canadian band's 2026 album Celebrate Another Day of Living. Mary & Adelaide describe themselves as a band from Oshawa, Ontario, and Canadian music press likewise identifies the group as Oshawa-based.

Toronto-based Alvvays turned jangly guitar pop, shoegaze texture and Molly Rankin's sharply observed songwriting into one of Canada's most internationally acclaimed indie catalogues. Ontario artist, producer and multi-instrumentalist Alysha Brilla has built a distinctly independent career blending soul, folk, pop and globally rooted rhythms. Edmonton-born, Ontario-raised singer-songwriter Alyssa Reid broke internationally with 2011's "Alone Again," a Canadian radio smash that later reached No. 2 in the U.K. and helped earn her a JUNO nomination for New Artist of the Year. Toronto singer Amanda Marshall became a defining Canadian pop-rock voice with a self-titled debut that went Diamond at home and produced a remarkable run of radio staples including "Let It Rain," "Birmingham" and "Dark Horse." Anachnid (1 track)

Montréal-based Oji-Cree and Mi'kmaq artist Anachnid blends experimental pop, electronic production and Indigenous storytelling into a highly distinctive multidisciplinary practice. Her 2020 debut Dreamweaver was longlisted for the Polaris Music Prize and helped lead to a 2021 Félix for Indigenous Artist of the Year. Songs such as "Windigo" and "Sky Woman" place spirituality, identity and contemporary urban Indigenous experience inside a modern electronic framework, making her an important bridge between Québec's alternative scene and a wider Indigenous music movement.

Bif Naked (6 tracks)

India-born and Winnipeg-raised Bif Naked brought punk-rooted individuality into Canadian mainstream rock through I Bificus and songs including "Spaceman," "Moment of Weakness" and "Lucky." Her career has combined alternative-rock hooks with an unusually candid public identity, later extending into memoir, health advocacy and animal-rights work. Decades after her 1990s breakthrough, anniversary releases and the Champion era have kept that independent streak active rather than nostalgic.

Winnipeg, Manitoba

Led by guitarist and producer Gordie Johnson, Big Sugar turned a collision of blues, hard rock, reggae and dub into one of the most distinctive sounds on 1990s Canadian rock radio. Albums including 500 Pounds and Hemi-Vision produced enduring songs such as "Diggin' a Hole" and "If I Had My Way," while the band's heavy live approach made roots music feel unusually physical and modern.

Big Wreck (8 tracks)

Big Wreck paired Ian Thornley's powerful voice and virtuosic guitar playing with a blend of alternative, progressive and blues rock that stood apart from much of late-1990s Canadian radio. The double-platinum In Loving Memory Of... produced "The Oaf," "That Song" and "Blown Wide Open." After an early-2000s split, Thornley revived the band and scored a No. 1 Canadian rock hit with "Albatross," beginning a productive second era that has continued through Ghosts, Grace Street, Pages and 2025's The Rest of the Story.

Toronto, Ontario

Mississauga’s Billy Talent turned years of local punk and alternative-rock groundwork into a national breakthrough with “Try Honesty” and the band’s 2003 self-titled album. Bran Van 3000 (31 tracks)

Montréal collective Bran Van 3000 turned the city's 1990s collision of hip-hop, electronic music, rock, soul and club culture into the JUNO-winning debut Glee. "Drinking in L.A." became an international signature song, while Discosis extended the collective's anything-goes approach through collaborators including Curtis Mayfield. The group's importance comes from treating genre-mixing as a natural expression of Montréal culture rather than a novelty, an approach later recognized when "Drinking in L.A." entered the Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame.

Montréal, Québec

Bryan Adams became one of Canada's defining international rock exports through the Jim Vallance songwriting partnership, 1983's Cuts Like a Knife and the blockbuster Reckless, home to "Run to You," "Summer of '69" and the U.S. No. 1 "Heaven." He later won a GRAMMY for "(Everything I Do) I Do It for You" and accumulated more than 20 JUNO wins. A 2006 Canadian Music Hall of Fame inductee, Adams remains an active touring artist and launched his own Bad Records label before releasing Roll with the Punches in 2025.

City and Colour (49 tracks)

City and Colour is Dallas Green's singer-songwriter project, launched alongside his work in Alexisonfire and built into a major Canadian career of its own. Sometimes introduced the intimate acoustic foundation, while Bring Me Your Love and the JUNO-winning Little Hell expanded the music into fuller folk-rock and soul-influenced arrangements. Later albums such as The Hurry and the Harm and If I Should Go Before You turned City and Colour into a full-band international touring act, showing how Green could move between post-hardcore intensity and deeply personal roots songwriting without diminishing either side.

St. Catharines, Ontario

Céline Dion turned a francophone Québec career into one of the largest international pop careers ever built by a Canadian artist. David Usher (9 tracks)

David Usher became one of Canada's recognizable 1990s alternative-rock voices as the frontman of Moist before establishing a substantial solo career of his own. After the multi-platinum *Silver* and *Creature*, he moved toward pop and electronic textures on records including *Little Songs* and the platinum, JUNO-winning *Morning Orbit*. The enduring "Black Black Heart" and his later return to Moist make Usher a rare example of two parallel, long-running Canadian music careers.

deadmau5 (7 tracks)

Niagara Falls-born producer Joel Zimmerman turned deadmau5 into one of the defining acts of the North American EDM boom. Random Album Title, For Lack of a Better Name and 4×4=12 established his slow-building progressive-house sound, while the mau5head, large-scale live production and mau5trap label expanded the project beyond records. Vancouver hard-rock band Default broke internationally with "Wasting My Time" and the platinum debut The Fallout, produced with early support from Chad Kroeger. Default's longevity makes the band a useful link between the western Canadian post-grunge boom and a later generation of crossover radio stars.

Dragonette (4 tracks)

Toronto electro-pop project Dragonette, centred on singer-songwriter Martina Sorbara, helped connect Canada's indie-electro scene with mainstream international dance-pop. Early albums Galore and Fixin to Thrill built the group's identity before the Martin Solveig collaboration "Hello" became a global hit and won the 2012 JUNO for Dance Recording of the Year. Later records including Bodyparts, Royal Blues and Twennies kept Dragonette focused on sophisticated synth-pop songwriting, while Sorbara's work for other artists broadened the project's influence beyond its own catalogue.

Toronto, Ontario

Drake (37 tracks)

Toronto's Drake moved from Degrassi and early mixtapes into one of the streaming era's defining rap careers. Thank Me Later debuted at No. 1, Take Care won the GRAMMY for Best Rap Album and later records including Views and Scorpion made his blend of rap, R&B and pop globally dominant. Just as important to Northern Dial's story, his OVO ecosystem and long collaboration with producer 40 helped make Toronto itself an internationally recognizable centre of contemporary hip-hop and R&B.

Dream Warriors (1 track)

Toronto's Dream Warriors helped push Canadian hip-hop onto the international stage with the jazz-rap landmark And Now the Legacy Begins. Their 1991 single "My Definition of a Boombastic Jazz Style" went gold in Canada, reached No. 13 in the U.K. and won the 1992 JUNO for Rap Recording of the Year. King Lou and Capital Q mixed jazz sampling, Caribbean sensibilities, humour and specifically Canadian references into a sound that offered an early alternative to imported rap templates. The song entered the Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2023.

Toronto, Ontario

Dubmatique (18 tracks)

Montréal pioneers Dubmatique helped make francophone hip-hop a mainstream force in Québec with the platinum 1997 debut La force de comprendre and the enduring single "Soul pleureur." Their breakthrough was so early that ADISQ initially honoured the album in an alternative-rock category before hip-hop had its own lane. Later recognized with major Félix honours and a SOCAN Classic Award, Dubmatique helped establish the commercial possibilities available to generations of Québec rappers.

Montréal, Québec

Vancouver's Econoline Crush brought industrial electronics into Canadian alternative and hard rock, moving from JUNO-recognized debut Purge through Affliction to the platinum breakthrough The Devil You Know. Toronto singer-songwriter Esthero helped blur the lines between trip-hop, R&B, jazz and alternative pop with the 1998 debut Breath from Another, a JUNO-nominated record that became a cult Canadian favourite. Fefe Dobson (6 tracks)

Scarborough singer-songwriter Fefe Dobson brought punk guitars and pop hooks into the early-2000s Canadian mainstream with songs such as "Take Me Away" and "Bye Bye Boyfriend." Her 2003 debut earned JUNO nominations, while her visibility as a Black woman in pop-punk gave her influence beyond the charts. After 2010's Joy and years of songwriting for other artists, she returned with Emotion Sickness in 2023, arriving amid a broader reassessment of her place in Canadian alternative-pop history.

Scarborough, Ontario

Vancouver producer Felix Cartal has evolved from late-2000s electro-house into one of Canada's most durable melodic dance-pop artists. Early albums Popular Music and Different Faces established his festival-era credentials, while Next Season and Expensive Sounds for Nice People shifted toward vocal-driven house. His Lights collaboration "Love Me" won the 2020 JUNO for Dance Recording of the Year, and later platinum singles reinforced a career built on adapting across multiple electronic-music eras without losing a strong pop songwriting instinct.

Burlington, Ontario's Finger Eleven evolved from the teenage Rainbow Butt Monkeys into a long-running alternative-rock band capable of repeatedly changing shape. Glenn Lewis (35 tracks)

Kitchener-born, Toronto-raised Glenn Lewis helped carry Canadian R&B into the international neo-soul boom of the early 2000s. After JUNO-nominated independent singles and work with Baby Blue Soundcrew, he signed to Epic and released World Outside My Window, which debuted at No. 4 on the Billboard 200. Its single "Don't You Forget It" became his signature hit and won a JUNO. Lewis's career remains a key bridge between Toronto's late-1990s urban scene and the city's later global R&B reputation.

Toronto, Ontario

Great Big Sea (1 track)

St. John's band Great Big Sea turned Newfoundland traditional music into a national folk-rock phenomenon without sanding away its regional identity. The self-titled debut and Up built a relentless touring audience before 1997's Play and "Ordinary Day" broke the group into the Canadian mainstream. Later albums including Turn and Sea of No Cares kept traditional repertoire beside original songs while the band became a major live draw. Their legacy lies in proving that Newfoundland language, history and communal music could sit at the centre of mainstream Canadian popular culture.

St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador

I Mother Earth (5 tracks)

Toronto's I Mother Earth brought funk, progressive rock, heavy alternative music and percussion-rich grooves together during Canada's 1990s rock boom. The Edwin-fronted Dig introduced the band's technical, rhythm-first approach, while the double-platinum Scenery and Fish produced "One More Astronaut," "Another Sunday" and "Used to Be Alright." Brian Byrne later fronted a second phase before the group went on hiatus. Their 2010s reunion confirmed a lasting place in Canadian rock for a band whose musicianship and fusion influences never fit neatly into standard post-grunge.

July Talk (2 tracks)

Toronto alternative-rock band July Talk built an instantly recognizable sound around the contrasting voices and stage presence of Leah Fay and Peter Dreimanis. Their self-titled debut went gold and won the 2015 JUNO for Alternative Album of the Year, while Touch expanded their mix of garage rock, blues and theatrical tension. Pray for It later earned another Alternative Album JUNO, and Remember Never Before pushed the group toward a more spacious, synth-aware sound without losing the charged vocal interplay at its core.

Junkhouse (1 track)

Hamilton's Junkhouse carried the city's blues-and-roots-heavy rock tradition onto national radio in the 1990s. Formed by Tom Wilson, the band broke through with 1993's *Strays* and "Out of My Head," then followed with *Birthday Boy* and *Fuzz*. Their rough-edged alternative rock, Sarah McLachlan collaboration and members' later work made Junkhouse an important bridge between Hamilton's older roots scene and the generations of nationally visible artists that followed.

Hamilton, Ontario

Edmonton-born singer Kreesha Turner broke through in 2008 with the top-10 Canadian single "Don't Call Me Baby" and debut album Passion, which earned JUNO nominations for New Artist and Pop Album of the Year. Her music moved among R&B, dance-pop and reggae influence, reflecting both her Canadian upbringing and Jamaican heritage. Later work including Tropic Electric pushed those Caribbean and dance elements further, making Turner a useful marker of Canadian pop's increasingly fluid genre boundaries in the late 2000s and early 2010s.

Edmonton, Alberta

Toronto group Len, led by siblings Marc and Sharon Costanzo, moved from independent alternative rock into a deliberately unruly mix of hip-hop, sampling, electronic music and pop. Toronto-formed MAGIC! turned reggae-pop into one of Canada's biggest international breakthroughs of the 2010s. Led by songwriter-producer Nasri Atweh, the band topped the Billboard Hot 100 for six weeks in 2014 with "Rude," the first Canadian-band No. 1 there since Nickelback's "How You Remind Me." Albums including Don't Kill the Magic, Primary Colours and Expectations extended the group's blend of pop, reggae and rock beyond its defining global hit.

Michie Mee (3 tracks)

Jamaica-born, Toronto-raised Michie Mee is one of the foundational figures in Canadian hip-hop. She became the first Canadian rapper to sign with a major U.S. label in 1988, then used 1991's Jamaican Funk – Canadian Style to fuse rap, reggae, dancehall and Jamaican patois years before that mix became central to Toronto's global musical identity. Her influence extends through later work with Raggadeath and a long independent career, and Canada Post honoured her with a commemorative hip-hop stamp in 2026.

Moist (7 tracks)

Vancouver's Moist was a central band in Canada's 1990s alternative-rock boom, breaking nationally with Silver and songs such as "Push" before expanding its reach with the JUNO-nominated Creature and Mercedes Five and Dime. Fronted by David Usher, the group paired dramatic vocals with atmospheric, radio-ready rock and became a major MuchMusic-era presence. After a long hiatus, Moist returned with Glory Under Dangerous Skies and End of the Ocean, extending a catalogue closely tied to Vancouver's role in Canadian alternative rock.

Muzion (14 tracks)

Montréal trio Muzion made Haitian-Québécois identity foundational to the sound and language of late-1990s Québec hip-hop. J.Kyll, Imposs and Dramatik moved among French, English and Haitian Creole on the Félix-winning albums Mentalité moune morne… (Ils n'ont pas compris) and J'rêvolutionne. Their kompa-inflected anthem "La vi ti nèg" later received SOCAN's Cultural Impact Award, while Canada Post honoured the group in its 2026 Canadian hip-hop stamp series. Muzion's influence helped later Black and immigrant artists see their own neighbourhoods and cultural references reflected in Québec music.

Montréal, Québec

Our Lady Peace (9 tracks)

Toronto's Our Lady Peace became one of the defining Canadian alternative-rock bands of the 1990s and early 2000s. Naveed introduced Raine Maida's unmistakable voice, while the Diamond-certified Clumsy produced "Superman's Dead," "Clumsy" and "4 AM." The band kept expanding through Happiness...Is Not a Fish That You Can Catch, the conceptual Spiritual Machines and the U.S.-crossing Gravity. Four JUNO wins, Summersault and a 2025 Canada's Walk of Fame induction reflect a career that helped make Canadian modern rock a national mainstream force.

Toronto, Ontario

Prozzäk (2 tracks)

Created by Philosopher Kings members Jay Levine and James Bryan McCollum, Prozzäk turned animated alter egos Simon and Milo into one of Canada's defining Y2K pop phenomena. The multi-platinum Hot Show produced "Sucks to Be You" and "Strange Disease," while Saturday People extended the duo's cartoon heartbreak universe and helped earn six JUNO nominations. Revived in the 2010s with Forever 1999, Prozzäk now reads as an unusually early Canadian example of a virtual pop act whose visual identity was inseparable from its songs.

Toronto, Ontario

Rascalz (39 tracks)

Vancouver's Rascalz helped move Canadian hip-hop from regional underground scenes toward a national conversation. Their 1997 album Cash Crop won a JUNO, but the group refused the award to protest rap's exclusion from the televised ceremony. A year later, the cross-country posse cut "Northern Touch" united Rascalz with Checkmate, Kardinal Offishall, Thrust and Choclair, won the 1999 JUNO and became one of Canadian rap's defining anthems. Their impact joined strong records with an industry-changing demand that hip-hop receive serious national visibility.

Vancouver, British Columbia

Remy Shand (1 track)

Winnipeg singer-songwriter and multi-instrumentalist Remy Shand made an unusually complete Canadian neo-soul statement with his 2002 debut The Way I Feel, which he wrote, arranged, produced and largely performed himself. The album reached No. 1 in Canada, won the 2003 JUNO for R&B/Soul Recording of the Year and generated four Grammy nominations, making his brief major-label run one of Canadian R&B's most distinctive early-2000s breakthroughs.

Rheostatics (1 track)

Toronto art-rock institution Rheostatics turned Canadian places, history and cultural mythology into some of the country's most adventurous guitar music. Melville and Whale Music became perennial critical favourites, while Music Inspired by the Group of Seven pushed their mix of rock, folk, progressive music and improvisation into an ambitious national-gallery commission. Their influence rests less on chart dominance than on showing how strange, specific and expansive Canadian rock could be.

Toronto, Ontario

Halifax singer-songwriter Ria Mae moved from Atlantic Canada's independent circuit into national pop with the Classified-produced "Clothes Off," a platinum hit that earned a JUNO nomination for Single of the Year. Burlington singer-songwriter Sarah Harmer moved from Ontario indie-rock band Weeping Tile into an acclaimed solo career with 2000's You Were Here. Mississauga singer, songwriter and dancer Shawn Desman helped define Canadian pop-R&B in the 2000s. Sloan (5 tracks)

Halifax-formed Sloan helped define 1990s Canadian indie rock through both its music and the Murderecords label it built around the East Coast scene. The unchanged quartet of Chris Murphy, Patrick Pentland, Jay Ferguson and Andrew Scott shares songwriting and lead vocals, giving albums such as Smeared, the JUNO-winning One Chord to Another and Navy Blues unusually varied personalities. More than three decades of lineup stability and independent-minded recording have made Sloan one of Canada's clearest examples of a band whose influence extends beyond its own songs into the infrastructure of a scene.

Halifax, Nova Scotia

Snow (51 tracks)

Toronto-born Snow turned the Caribbean musical environment of North York into one of Canada's strangest and biggest early-1990s crossover stories. His debut 12 Inches of Snow produced "Informer," a seven-week Billboard Hot 100 No. 1 that fused dancehall, reggae and rap at global pop scale. Later albums leaned more directly into Jamaican production, while Daddy Yankee's 2019 "Con Calma" revived the song for a new generation. "Informer" entered the Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2023.

Toronto, Ontario

soulDecision (2 tracks)

Vancouver trio soulDecision mixed pop, R&B and dance production during the turn-of-the-millennium teen-pop boom. Their 2000 debut No One Does It Better produced "Ooh It's Kinda Crazy" and the Canadian No. 1 "Faded," which also brought the group U.S. radio exposure. Often marketed beside boy bands, soulDecision stood apart through Trevor Guthrie's songwriting and a stronger blue-eyed-soul influence, making the group an important Canadian crossover act just before the country's later global pop surge.

Tanya Tagaq (2 tracks)

Ikaluktutiak-born Inuk artist Tanya Tagaq turned solo throat singing into an uncompromising experimental language spanning voice, electronics, improvisation, literature and visual art. Her album Animism won the 2014 Polaris Music Prize, while Retribution, Tongues and 2026's Saputjiji pushed further into colonial critique, environmental politics and industrial sound. A Member of the Order of Canada and award-winning author of Split Tooth, Tagaq has helped expand the international space available to contemporary Inuit art without separating experimentation from cultural and political urgency.

Tegan and Sara (49 tracks)

Calgary twins Tegan and Sara Quin grew from acoustic and indie-rock beginnings into an internationally influential pop duo. So Jealous and The Con built their indie audience, while 2013's Heartthrob and the hit "Closer" brought a deliberate synth-pop breakthrough and three JUNO Awards. Their career has also carried unusual cultural weight through longstanding queer visibility, the Tegan and Sara Foundation and the 2024 JUNO Humanitarian Award, making them important not only as songwriters but as advocates who widened the space available to LGBTQ+ artists in Canadian popular music.

Calgary, Alberta

Ottawa's The Halluci Nation, formerly A Tribe Called Red, transformed the Electric Pow Wow parties into an internationally influential fusion of powwow singing and drumming, electronic production, hip-hop and bass music. The Philosopher Kings (32 tracks)

Toronto-area band The Philosopher Kings brought jazz-trained musicianship into Canadian R&B, soul and pop during the 1990s. Their self-titled debut won the 1996 JUNO for Best R&B/Soul Recording, while Famous, Rich and Beautiful produced the hit "Hurts to Love You" and further JUNO recognition. The group's influence also spread through its members: Gerald Eaton became producer Jarvis Church, while James Bryan McCollum and Jason Levine created Prozzäk, making the band an important incubator for later Canadian pop and R&B.

The Tea Party (3 tracks)

Windsor trio The Tea Party gave 1990s Canadian alternative rock one of its most distinctive vocabularies, combining heavy guitars and progressive structures with Middle Eastern, Indian and North African instruments and scales. Splendor Solis and the multi-platinum The Edges of Twilight established the band, while Transmission and Triptych pushed into industrial and more polished rock territory. Scarborough-born Abel Tesfaye emerged anonymously in 2011 with House of Balloons and helped define the shadowy alternative-R&B sound that made Toronto newly influential. Virginia to Vegas (2 tracks)

Virginia to Vegas, the pop project of Derik John Baker, broke through with the Alyssa Reid collaboration "We Are Stars" after signing to Toronto's Wax Records. He turned that start into a sustained run of Canadian hits including "Lights Out," "Selfish," "Just Friends" and "betterman," earning multi-platinum certifications and a JUNO nomination. Albums Utopian and Don't Wake Me, I'm Dreaming anchor a catalogue built on melodic electronic production and unusually consistent radio songwriting.

Walk Off the Earth (4 tracks)

Burlington's Walk Off the Earth turned inventive performance videos into an international career after their five-people-one-guitar cover of "Somebody That I Used to Know" went viral in 2012. They followed with original hits such as "Red Hands," the albums R.E.V.O. and Sing It All Away and a 2016 JUNO for Group of the Year. Their combination of multi-instrumental arrangements, visual experimentation and pop songwriting made them a defining Canadian success story of the YouTube era.

William Prince (2 tracks)

Peguis First Nation singer-songwriter William Prince built his resonant folk-country style from music learned alongside his preacher father at church services, wakes and funerals across Manitoba. His debut Earthly Days won the 2017 JUNO for Contemporary Roots Album of the Year, beginning a catalogue that later included Reliever, Gospel First Nation, Stand in the Joy and 2025's Further From the Country. A two-time JUNO winner and John Prine Songwriter Fellowship recipient, Prince pairs a commanding baritone with restrained writing about family, grief, place and the distance between home and a growing international career.

Peguis First Nation, Manitoba
